Topology events also report relationship changes to other components. The remaining bonded-state validation conjunction is still being traced, so the object model alone does not specify every condition under which a proposed bond is accepted.
subsystems.ibt_plans: IBT ('intended targets') is how cloud-issued household commands fan out to specific players: a command arriving over the cloud channel is compiled into a 'plan' naming which players execute it. This entry covers the plan format and how plans get built and run.
subsystems.lechmere_wss: The persistent secure-websocket channel between player and cloud, internally called 'lechmere'. It's the always-on pipe that cloud commands and modern-API calls arrive over, using a compact binary message format inside standard web framing. It's the link that makes your speaker controllable from anywhere, not just your home network.
subsystems.led_engine: Drives indicator lights using programs made of color steps, hold and fade durations, repeat counts and selected LED identifiers. Player states such as setup, mute or an error select a default pattern, while priority, brightness and pattern completion affect what is shown next. Hardware features determine which lights and brightness controls a model has. The ordinary status-light preference is one input to this system rather than a description of every indicator animation.
subsystems.log_domain_map: Maps the player's log files and category names to the areas that produce diagnostic output. Examples separate transport playback, home theater, hardware events, Spotify, modern-API commands and events, and line-in activity; sibling daemons have their own logs. A filename is an output sink, while a log-domain label identifies a category within the logging system, so the two should not be counted as identical module boundaries. The vocabulary is mapped, but the complete call-site inventory for every domain remains open.
subsystems.media_player_abstraction: Provides shared interfaces through which the transport layer works with different source implementations, including local inputs, home theater, virtual line-in and auxiliary sounds. The player manager selects and tracks the appropriate source, while autoplay and session-control components manage its transitions. Sharing an interface does not make every source support identical operations or failure behavior. Concrete source-to-interface bindings are still being traced in this record, and capability checks remain important for any particular command.
subsystems.model_sku_vocabulary: Identifies the product and submodel codes used to select model-specific configuration and capabilities. Entries distinguish hardware features such as input and output types, so a common firmware image can contain paths for equipment absent from the current device. Display-name and SKU records help relate those codes to product variants. Several capability-tuple fields and flags still lack proven meanings, so the table should not be read as a fully decoded feature matrix for every model.
subsystems.multi_daemon_boundary: This program is one daemon of about thirteen on the player. It pushes network settings to the network-startup daemon over a local socket and receives connection updates back, while LED, Bluetooth, and power behavior live in their own daemons. Most device behaviors are actually owned by these siblings, and this layer marks where this program's job ends and theirs begins.
subsystems.muse_semantics: The 'muse' API is Sonos's real product API: the REST-style surface the app talks to over the cloud and websocket channel. Hundreds of routes are catalogued, covering every classic command reachable through it plus modern-only features the old surface never had. This is the vocabulary of what the API can mean, not just its URL list.
subsystems.play_history: Turns observed track playback into listening-history entries for the household history service. A recorder follows track identity, position and boundaries, buffers entries and submits them when the required information is complete; a full buffer can drop entries. Reading history uses a cached response, while separate operations remove individual items or clear history. Ratings have a distinct cloud-queue implementation and should not be assumed to apply to every playback source. The exact posted entry nesting still needs its remaining trace.
subsystems.playlist_parsers: Reads playlist or manifest resources before the player chooses individual tracks or streaming segments. Recovered parsers handle ASX references, M3U, WLP and PLS lists, while HLS handling tracks variants, segment sequence, bitrate and encryption information. Candidate renditions can be rejected for missing addresses, unsupported codecs, bandwidth or audio capabilities. Reading a playlist therefore supplies possible resources; it does not guarantee that every entry can be played or that every external playlist is importable into a saved Sonos queue.
subsystems.qplay_protocol: The QPlay protocol implementation: the wire details of the Tencent casting protocol, including the seed-and-code exchange and the session flow. It's one of the private protocols sitting alongside the documented services, and it's how a Tencent-linked client pushes music at the player.
subsystems.queue_persistence: Saves queue entries as resource addresses and metadata so the player can reload its selected queue data. Saved playlists use savedqueues.rsq, with playlist identifiers and track records, while the live queue has a separate trackqueue.rsq backup. Temporary-file replacement and backup files support writes, and loaded or replicated data is checked for compatible, playable entries. These stores do not copy the audio files themselves, and a saved reference may later be unavailable. The four-byte current-play-state file is separate crash-diagnostic data, not a saved playback queue.
subsystems.runtime_flag_files: Lists temporary and runtime files that communicate state between components. Some are presence markers, such as device-unlocked, broken-device or wireless-disabled state; others contain data, such as the crash-time audio activity mask, runtime modes, preserved event records or log buffers. Scratch files and temporary SMB mount directories have still different purposes. The owning reader or writer determines the effect of each path, so creating every listed file would not be one interchangeable way to toggle a feature.
subsystems.scrobbler: Submits listening-history entries to the Audioscrobbler/Last.fm integration. The legacy flow first obtains a session through a handshake, then sends form fields for artist, title, listening timestamp, source, track length, album, track number and music identifier. A BADTIME handshake response can lead it to use the server's HTTP Date header for time recovery, and the response must indicate success. A newer API and mobile-session authentication are also present. Account selection, submission-trigger details and parts of signing remain unresolved, so this is not proof that every finished track is reported.
subsystems.semisleep_power: Coordinates lower-power suspension on devices that support it and have the relevant configuration enabled. Suspension affects playback and virtual-line-in sessions, group-member handling and operations on local timers; paused timers retain their remaining duration and pause time in storage. Wake and prevent-idle guards let selected operations hold the device out of sleep while they run. The record identifies these interacting paths, but does not establish one identical suspend or wake sequence for every model.
subsystems.settings_replication: Synchronizes selected household stores such as accounts, network configuration, favorites, saved queues and location or area data between players. Transfers identify the setting, version and format, and receivers check encoding, schema and related admission conditions before installing data. Invalid items can be denied, while registration or quarantine state can suppress particular replication paths. These checks distinguish a new local value, its announcement to peers and its successful installation elsewhere. The supported stores and receiver conditions determine what is actually shared.
subsystems.sntp_server: Provides time synchronization as both a client and a household server. A player can obtain time from the Sonos time-server pool or a group-related source and expose a clock for other players to query. Server and virtual-clock registration, monitoring and removal are managed separately, with errors when a clock or port cannot be installed. Playback scheduling checks whether the synchronization state is valid. The remaining server-election rule and jitter or drift thresholds are still being traced; synchronization support alone is not a guarantee that every playback instance is perfectly aligned.
subsystems.spotify_esdk: Connects Spotify playback commands and SDK callbacks to the Sonos player. Commands cover play, pause, seeking, skipping and active-device selection; callbacks supply connection state, credentials, stream start and flush information, playback notifications, position queries and errors. The integration also advertises Spotify discovery and manages login or logout when switching to another source mode. Handoff can request a seek and wait for audio to start, and that wait can time out. These stages distinguish a command being accepted from the SDK successfully delivering its new stream.
subsystems.telemetry_submission: Packages and sends selected player reports, while the support-diagnostics flow submits artifacts and a final manifest. Telemetry events carry category and context fields and can identify their message type as product-data telemetry. Configuration can affect particular report families or positioning telemetry level, and some report paths have consent exemptions. The concrete host is resolved from runtime service configuration rather than one fixed address in this record. The reporting-policy and diagnostics-submission records describe the individual permission and completion rules.
subsystems.trueplay_tuning: Coordinates speaker discovery, tuning configuration and calibration status used by the room-tuning paths. The player can play predefined test sounds, retrieve spectral or spatial tuning assets, apply configuration and propagate calibration status to satellite speakers. The firmware also includes self-tuning and room-adaptation related variants. Asset versions, compatibility and configuration validation matter before tuning data is applied. The remaining state names and parameter units prevent treating the route inventory as a complete description of how every measurement is computed.
subsystems.update_machinery: Uses an update manifest to identify the target firmware for each player's model, submodel and software generation. A user-initiated household update downloads the manifest, checks participating devices and then launches the eligible updates; automatic updating adds policy, interval and window checks. A manifest can require manual updating for a model or an installed version below its automatic-update minimum. Related downloads update supporting data such as time-zone tables or calibration tones. Progress and per-device results must be checked separately from successfully finding an offered version.
subsystems.wac_mode: Tracks the Wi-Fi accessory-configuration mode used by the network-setup components. The mode is recorded in a runtime file, and netstartd messages report enable, disable, timeout and setup-state transitions. The player also receives SSID set or clear events and selects a WAC-related indicator pattern. This separates the control program's setup-state handling from the credential exchange performed by the network daemons. The recorded WAC mode does not establish that every onboarding or recovery flow uses this same protocol.
subsystems.device_unlock: Handles local development or manufacturing unlock state. The available endpoints can set the unlocked marker and expose status, while the challenge-response flow has per-device attempt checks and can initiate a reboot after success. Locked and unlocked states affect which web content is served. Diagnostic helpers can also test unlocked state and refuse particular self-tests. An unlock endpoint being present is different from an arbitrary request successfully obtaining the required unlocked state.
subsystems.testenv_environment: Changes the configured backend environment among production, performance, staging, test and integration choices. The form displays resolved bases for cloud, service catalog, system, transfer, metrics and update services and allows a separate online-update URL override. Changes pass through replicated settings so other household players can learn them; the page warns that propagation may take up to about two minutes. That notice describes the intended replication delay, not proof that an offline peer has already received the new values.
subsystems.abr_engine: Selects and fetches a suitable bitrate variant for a segmented stream using the available playlist, estimated transfer rate and buffered audio. It can fetch a new playlist, switch sources or reduce bitrate when download progress cannot sustain the current choice. Minimum and maximum variants bound the available choices. Recovery can still fail when playlists are empty, a fetch times out or too little audio remains buffered. The engine tries to maintain delivery; it does not guarantee that every poor connection becomes dropout-free.
subsystems.aha_ops: Names the audio-session operations used to stop or restore a path and to end, suspend or pause a virtual-line-in session. They relate to the channel logger and group-advertisement activity associated with that audio path. Source diagnostics distinguish line-in, dock, virtual and coordinator-supplied music sources. The remaining payload fields vary by source and still require their producer traces. The AHA vocabulary here belongs to audio-session management rather than establishing a legacy music-service partner integration.
subsystems.amp_manager: Uses playback, volume, fixed-output and preemptive-start information to manage the amplifier's power and mute state. It can request power-on, unmute, mute, power-off or a high/low power-rail transition, with separate handling when the hardware does not support an operation. The off decision considers several state inputs and can schedule a delayed power-off instead of turning off immediately. Status-change events and failed hardware calls expose the outcome, so requesting an amplifier transition is separate from it succeeding.
subsystems.ap_layer: Maintains the Spotify access-point connection used by the embedded Spotify client. It resolves a server address, opens a connection, sends the protocol handshake and login data, and processes server packets with length and integrity checks. Lost connectivity can disconnect it and later trigger reconnection, while an absent response or permanent connection error has its own failure path. AP in this record refers to Spotify's service connection, not the speaker acting as a wireless access point.
subsystems.async_stream: Buffers media data in segments and blocks while asynchronous reads fetch upcoming content. Playback and pause positions identify which cached bytes can be consumed or retained, and the stream can release already-played blocks to satisfy later allocations. Once released, those bytes are no longer available for fast backward scrubbing without another read. The implementation also checks end-of-file ordering and outstanding I/O before deleting a segment. This is the media-stream buffering path; it does not establish that event channels use the same buffer.
subsystems.audio_clip: Schedules a short sound using a clip type, priority, playback behavior and optional light behavior. Built-in buzzer clips use packaged audio files, while a custom clip requires a stream URL; supplying HTTP authorization also requires a secure URL. Delivery can use transport playback or an external-audio source, and policy can refuse interrupting an existing higher-priority clip or require current content to pause first. A clip identifier supports later cancellation and result tracking. These choices prevent treating every clip request as an unconditional overlay on music.
subsystems.audio_decoder: Reads an audio resource through the selected decoder and produces sample blocks with a known sample rate, bit depth, channel count and layout. It handles initialization, headers, position queries and seeking, including a time-based fallback when a saved byte position exceeds the current file. Bad input, unsupported sample properties, repeated errors, no progress or an unexpected end of file can stop the decode path. Recognizing a media type is therefore a different stage from decoding that particular resource successfully.
subsystems.audio_decoders: Collects the format-specific decoder implementations and their validation rules. Vorbis handling checks configuration, available bytes and produced samples, while AAC handling interprets object type, frequency and channel information and can reject unsupported forms. Other records cover the remaining MP3, FLAC and ALAC paths. Each format has its own initialization, seek and failure behavior, so the player's general format vocabulary does not make all decoder variants interchangeable.
subsystems.audio_fifo: Keeps ordered audio records in the Spotify/eSDK playback path while production and consumption run at different times. Records track positions and contiguous ranges; a write at the wrong pending offset, too few free records or a discontinuity can fail or force different handling. Reads advance across contiguous data and recognize end-of-file or logical-track boundaries. Prebuffering waits for enough audio before proceeding, with timing and fullness diagnostics. Its behavior is specific to this FIFO rather than a guarantee that every network delay is hidden.
subsystems.audio_rate_ctrl: Adjusts sample-rate conversion according to the incoming audio clock and measured timing drift. It validates channel counts and audio or line rates, resets or reconfigures on a change, and limits the correction when drift reaches configured bounds. Missing measurements, a zero adjustment rate, out-of-range excursion or conversion failure can report an error or mute-related condition. The conversion paths reuse the common filter table described under sounddev. Several control-loop constants still lack a fully established semantic interpretation.
subsystems.audio_stream_mixer: Coordinates input streams and output timing in the playback and DSP path. Streams can start buffering, receive a presentation time, resynchronize, drain or skip old buffered audio, while fade records move gain toward a target over a sample interval. The mixer also manages output latency, driver draining and completion state, with explicit failures for exhausted fade slots or inconsistent buffering. It supplies mechanisms used by multiple sources; a source-specific policy still decides whether two particular sounds are mixed, paused or replaced.
subsystems.audio_tap: Offers named capture points inside the audio-processing path, such as line-in, codec output, mixer output, DSP output and external-voice or chirp streams. A request must select a valid, permitted location, and the manager rejects duplicate captures or capacity exhaustion. These taps expose the samples at a chosen stage for diagnosis, rather than only the command that requested playback. The separate rolling SPDIF snapshot is compressed and needs decompression before replay; capture-format fields are documented in audio_taps.
subsystems.audioin_groups: Tracks audio-input transmission groups by their coordinator identifier. Adding a group checks for duplicates and available capacity, while stopping transmission can fail when the named coordinator is not in the group table. The stream vocabulary distinguishes compressed, uncompressed and virtual-SPDIF paths, and demo mode can force uncompressed audio. These are internal source and group-management behaviors; their presence does not establish that every public AudioIn operation is enabled on this model.
subsystems.audiotap_manager: Manages asynchronous audio-capture requests and the lifetime of their selected tap locations. A request can fail to start, cannot consume data after it has closed, and can report a write failure while capture is active. Location checks reject ineligible or already-tapped sources and enforce capacity, while diagnostics show active and closing captures. The typed debug fields describe channel names and floating-point, text or integer values. Tap scheduling and eligibility are separate from the compressed SPDIF snapshot-file format.
subsystems.bandwidth_meter: Calculates transfer bandwidth from the number of bytes received and the elapsed time in the Spotify/eSDK download path. It also maintains a measurement window and records observations below a configured bandwidth threshold. A zero-latency sample is skipped rather than divided into a rate, and inconsistent request or completion timestamps are checked. The resulting numbers describe observed transfer progress; a separate streaming policy decides whether or how to change the selected bitrate.
subsystems.bt_sbc: Decodes SBC audio packets in the Bluetooth receive path. Configuration includes sample frequency, block count, subbands, channel mode, allocation method and bitpool, which together determine the compressed frame layout. Invalid headers, truncated packets, changed frame sizes or unsuccessful decoding produce distinct errors. This documents the software decoder path; it does not prove that the examined player has an active Bluetooth input or that every Bluetooth configuration is accepted.
subsystems.cdn_fetcher: Downloads Spotify media chunks from the supplied CDN addresses using a requested offset and size. It follows redirects and can retry a timeout or read failure or move to another CDN when the current one fails. Reads also check end-of-file behavior and available destination-buffer space, with explicit unrecoverable or write-failure paths. Completion records bytes and elapsed time. Retry and failover offer recovery mechanisms, but they do not guarantee uninterrupted playback after every failed download.
subsystems.chirp: Encodes a payload into audio tones using the Sonos CDMA profile in the Chirp libraries. The linked implementation contains symbol codebooks, error-correction and decoder components such as peak detection, note estimation, scoring and voting. The recovered player usage is sender-only; linked decode routines do not establish an active phone-to-speaker receive workflow. The source record does not prove that this build transmits Wi-Fi credentials from a phone or identify every payload field, so those app scenarios should not be inferred from the library names.
subsystems.chirp_sdk: Provides the Chirp SDK objects, profiles and sample-processing routines used by the player's acoustic sender path. Configuration describes modulation, message sizes and audio-channel behavior, while the send routine turns a payload into output samples. The library also includes decode APIs and error messages, but the recovered call reachability on this build is sender-only. The remaining payload-encoding semantics belong to the underlying Chirp core; a list of exported routines is not proof that each is exposed as a player feature.
subsystems.chsnk: Receives framed group audio and prepares it for local playback. The sink tracks buffered audio and timing differences from the coordinator, and it handles crossfade data, volume-normalization ramps, discontinuities and underflow conditions. Those measurements and controls support synchronized output while giving diagnostics separate indicators for fill level and clock mismatch. The packet header is recovered, but the field grammar for every payload type remains open. Receiving a stream is not a guarantee that every packet arrives or every transition stays perfectly aligned.
subsystems.chsnk_detail: Handles the buffered transition from one channel-audio source to another, including local or remote handoff. It compares old and new frame identities and offsets, waits for compatible data and can complete a quick or delayed transition or time out. Time synchronization must become valid before certain playback steps proceed, and a backwards local clock or network read error has its own handling path. These checks explain why a requested seamless handoff can succeed, wait, fall back or fail rather than being only a source-name change.
subsystems.chsrc_chsnk: Connects the audio-producing group source with the receiving sinks on other players. The source manages playback work and emits framed data; the sink receives and decodes that data into its local playback path. Frame identifiers, timestamps, offsets and control information let the two sides follow track or source transitions and request recovery where supported. The shared framing is documented, while meanings of remaining packed fields and payload types still require their producer and consumer traces.
subsystems.crossfade: Overlaps samples from an outgoing and incoming stream during a fade transition. The implementation tracks the remaining samples, time alignment and gain ramps and has separate paths for different sample representations. Empty or underflowing streams, incompatible types or timestamps too far in the past can prevent the intended overlap or cause fallback handling. Enabling a user crossfade preference is therefore distinct from having two eligible, sufficiently buffered streams at the transition.
subsystems.dolby_decoder: Decodes the supported Dolby input path and loads Dolby Audio Processing configuration used alongside it. Configuration can come from the firmware file, a writable debug override or default presets and contains static speaker or mode choices plus dynamic filters and processing values. Decoder status exposes sample rate, channel count and low-frequency-channel presence. Parsing, initialization or decode failures have separate errors. The compiled vocabulary does not establish that every Dolby format or preset is available on every product.
subsystems.evo_decoder: Provides the Dolby Evolution and DDPI processing path identified by the recovered allocation, initialization and metadata operations. It first queries required static or dynamic memory and can fail to allocate or initialize that storage. Processing then obtains frame or timeslice metadata and reports malformed signals, extraction failures or driver-completion errors. These are concrete processing stages, but their presence alone does not prove that the examined hardware supports every newer Dolby or Atmos input format.
subsystems.lla: Connects the player's audio code to low-level device operations. It opens the selected device, obtains buffer limits, requests transmit latency and queries device time or output delay to relate a write to its intended playback time. Results distinguish a temporarily blocked operation, underflow or overflow, invalid data and suspension. Timing diagnostics expose data already scheduled in the past or driver queries that failed. Higher layers use those outcomes when deciding to wait, reset or report a playback error.
subsystems.tdm_driver: Identifies the TDM and SPDIF driver path that opens /dev/dsp, requests the audio-bus mode and maps driver memory into the process. The implementation reports separate failures for opening, mode setup, memory mapping and unmapping. It also recognizes SPDIF block restart and oversized-block conditions. These operations describe one hardware-facing audio path, rather than establishing that every output on every product ultimately uses the same driver.
subsystems.circuit_breaker: This protects the speaker from repeatedly contacting a failing cloud service. Six failures within two minutes pause new attempts for 30 seconds. The next check then permits retries, and a successful response clears the failure history. The retry threshold counts failed results, not requests in flight. A received HTTP error response can still count as a successful connection, because the callers check whether a response arrived rather than whether it was a 2xx response. Its telemetry label successful retries actually counts openings of the retry state; it does not count successful retry responses.
subsystems.cloud: Collects the player-side helpers for cloud HTTP calls, registration changes, account authorization and secure-connection cache maintenance. A response can fail because a stream cannot be opened, the HTTP result is unsuitable, a body is incomplete or JSON parsing fails. Account transactions can wait for refreshed authorization, while cached TLS state has its own clock, idle-state and configuration checks. These mechanisms support individual cloud features; they do not mean that every player function needs internet access or that all outbound traffic uses one connection.
subsystems.cloud_api_paths: Inventories URL families constructed for cloud operations, including tokens, invitations, users, account subscriptions, downloads and product-event reports. Household, player, service, user and group prefixes identify the scope of the target, while query values can carry account identifiers, update versions, object identifiers or download information. This gives concrete addresses and parameter vocabulary to follow in the corresponding feature records. The presence of a builder does not establish the method, permission rules or complete response body for every operation.
subsystems.cloud_registration: Updates the player's cloud-registration information when its network, household or session context changes. The recovered required data includes the registered device identity, household location, DHCP-server hardware address, player IP address and household name. If required information is missing, registration work is deferred rather than sent with a complete-looking record. Cached registration events and a wireless-monitor job keep changes associated with that process. This record describes those update inputs and triggers, not a universal rule that every unregistered player feature is local-only.
subsystems.cloud_services: Maps service names to the host or URL templates resolved for their functions. Names distinguish registration, feature configuration, music history, account services, recommendations, search, crash upload and the persistent event channel, among others. Different environment settings can select different concrete hosts from those templates. The registry helps trace where a particular request is directed; the exact service-to-environment binding at a deployment remains configuration data, so the names alone cannot diagnose the cause of every outage.
subsystems.cloud_synchronizer: Runs event-driven synchronization work through a registry of services. Registration has a capacity limit and a guard against registering the service set more than once; the worker receives events and can discard types it does not handle. The individual registered service determines which data to fetch or apply. Its complete registrant list and event-body schema remain unresolved, so this entry does not establish that all settings, accounts and playlists are mirrored or that replacement players can restore every item from the cloud.
subsystems.cert: Checks the metadata associated with a device certificate and records certificate retrieval or refresh outcomes. Failures distinguish a missing or bad file, key or certificate, an unsuitable issue date and mismatches in environment, issuer, household or user. Metadata records also include request time, download status, HTTP status and the previous ETag, separating a new download from an unchanged result. Unknown metadata state can schedule a refresh, while missing UTC time or an expired certificate affects the relevant validation path.
subsystems.cert_files: Identifies files that hold certificate material, an encrypted private key, expiration information and the key-encryption type. The reader uses those pieces together to obtain the identity required by a particular secure connection or signing operation; a key-retrieval failure is a separate result from a certificate simply being present. The recovered decrypt path uses the established ECB raw-key form. Whether the shipped artifacts contain an active CBC variant remains unresolved, so that variant should not be assumed from its name alone.
subsystems.cert_layer: Organizes certificate-store files under an identity-specific directory and, where selected, an environment namespace. The recovered registration-device store uses a regdevicecert family, with prod as the fallback environment. Updating certificate material can write a temporary file and rename it into place, while loading a replacement has its own size and failure checks. This storage and replacement layer is distinct from interpreting a certificate's issuer, household and user metadata in the validation paths.
subsystems.devicecertmanager: Downloads and refreshes device-certificate material and tracks the result of each attempt. It uses cached ETag information to distinguish a changed download from an unchanged response and records request timing, HTTP and download status. Missing files can enter a generation path, and unknown metadata state can cause a refresh job to be scheduled. Validation errors identify unusable keys, dates or identity context. The concrete registration-service base URL is resolved for the configured environment rather than fixed in this record.
subsystems.hermes: Carries Spotify control and service messages on named Hermes resource channels. Subscriptions include device state, volume, play, shuffle, repeat and queue updates, alongside content-encryption-key, cache-key and restriction resources. Incoming messages require header decoding and can be fragmented, while requests can be held during a server-imposed rate limit. The recovered channel names identify these functions; the complete numeric header-tag assignments remain unresolved in the embedded descriptor.
subsystems.jwt_auth: Parses, generates or validates JWT credentials used by selected device and modern-API authentication paths. Failures distinguish malformed encoded data, an invalid header or payload, an unsupported algorithm, an invalid signature and an untrusted certificate chain. Device or guest token generation also has trusted-time and credential prerequisites, and PIN-based paths use nonce checks. A validated token is an input to authorization rather than proof that every operation is permitted. Key-material storage and rotation details remain unresolved.
subsystems.lechmere: The persistent cloud pipe, internally named 'lechmere': the always-on channel carrying modern-API commands in and device events out, with route templates defining its addressing. It's the link between your speaker and Sonos's servers that works even when you're away from home.
subsystems.muse: The 'muse' layer: Sonos's internal name for the modern API machinery as a whole, covering the route tables, router, operation objects, and pipeline documented on the modern-API page.
subsystems.muse_engine: The modern-API engine: the namespace registry, request validation, fan-out to target players, authorization, and execution, mounted on the API routes and the cloud pipe. It's the counterpart of the classic command machinery for the app's REST-style world.
subsystems.muse_errors: Enumerates named results used by the modern API, including successful creation, acceptance, no-content and not-modified outcomes as well as failures. Error families distinguish unavailable or unplayable content, expired credentials, session eviction, account problems, insufficient update power and invalid configuration. These categories help a client identify what kind of failure occurred without interpreting a free-text log. The exact triggering condition and whether a result means work was submitted or completed still belong to the individual operation.
subsystems.muse_events: Lists named updates available to modern-API subscribers, including playback status, volume, group changes, alarms, sleep timers, registration, wireless status and tuning. Some names announce a data-version change rather than supplying the entire changed collection, so the event schema determines what a client should fetch or update afterwards. A subscription lets the player deliver the relevant changes without repeated state queries. Hardware capability and producer behavior still determine which topics can generate updates for a particular device.
subsystems.muse_field_schema: Inventories JSON field names used across modern-API objects. Concrete groups cover credentials and protocol context, battery charge and temperature, player identity and network information, audio-input sources, and playback capability flags such as whether skipping or pausing is available. These are machine-readable keys rather than display labels. The vocabulary establishes spelling and domains; a specific object schema is still needed to know which fields are required, their types and when they are present.
subsystems.muse_logging: Identifies the modern API's command and event logging categories and examples of operations recorded there. The recovered operation names include loading an audio clip, starting direct control, updating protected administrative settings and creating a voice account. These records can help relate an API operation to surrounding events or errors. Logging an operation name does not establish that every supplied value is logged or that sensitive credentials are safe to infer from the diagnostic output.
subsystems.muse_perf: Measures stages of modern-API processing and reports their durations, average times and observation counts. Named stages separate authorization, token parsing, policy-cache retrieval, command parsing, dispatch, execution, logging and reporting; a volume-setting stage is also identified. This makes a slow authorization path distinguishable from work in execution rather than reducing both to one command timeout. The profiler describes measured stages, while the operation's own result still determines success or failure.
subsystems.muse_target_validator: The gate that resolves a command's target: implicit targets (the receiving player), explicit targets (another player or group by ID), and the rejections for unauthorized or missing targets. This is the first thing a command hits after auth, and most client-error failures originate here.
subsystems.muse_types: Lists the named object types used by modern-API specification fields, such as alarm descriptions, active-zone members, account errors and settings objects. A type name identifies an object shape that can be referenced from a field specification; it is different from the field name or the event topic. Several bridge namespaces use an upnpEvent wrapper for status values. The registry helps interpret those references but is not, by itself, a complete field-by-field wire schema for every named type.
subsystems.muse_verbs: The verb-name table: every operation callable per namespace, hundreds of them across all the resource groups. This is effectively the full modern-API method list, the operation vocabulary the route table can invoke.
subsystems.muse_enums: Collects named choices used by modern-API fields, including actor roles, credential types, content classes, playback states, queue-insertion actions and ratings. A queue action such as append, insert-next or play-now expresses a different requested placement, while paused, playing and buffering describe playback state. Permission and business-tier names are also vocabulary inputs to their policy consumers. Their presence in the table does not establish that a caller holds the named permission or that a particular player supports every listed content type.
subsystems.ibt: Intended-target fan-out: a single modern-API command can name a set of target players, and this planner expands it into per-target executions after validating that the command supports fan-out and each target parses. This is how the app sends one 'set volume' to a whole room instead of issuing per-player calls.
subsystems.ibt_planner: The planner half of intended-target execution: when a cloud command names its players, this generates the target list and parses whether targets were explicit or implied. It's the routing brain that turns 'command X for the household' into 'command X for these specific speakers'.
subsystems.inprocess_events: Keeps the named observer registrations that let components react to a subject changing inside the player process. Registration and removal update the observer count, and different observer families support immediate, scheduled or cached delivery. Playback and power-related components use this mechanism alongside their own state and timeout checks. An internal observer registration is separate from a client's network subscription, even when a later handler turns that change into an API event.
subsystems.network: Collects the player-side components for saved network configuration, key rotation, network-daemon communication and connectivity tests. Configuration changes carry a version and can update household, control, room-encryption and network-swap keys before being pushed to netstartd. A SonosNet-disable test can schedule an automatic revert when the changed configuration is not confirmed, while a separate network test records its connection or re-enable outcome. These are distinct stateful operations rather than one generic socket interface.
subsystems.network_tools: Serves diagnostic forms that ask the player to run ping, traceroute, name lookup or a discovery reannouncement. The host input and form token are passed through the relevant request path, and the ping command uses three probes in the recovered template. A packet-capture path streams a trace file as a download and excludes traffic for the specified host/port pair. These tools collect or trigger specific network observations; they do not automatically repair a failed connection.
subsystems.authz: The authorization machinery: the component that checks credentials on incoming requests, covering API keys on the modern surface and permission checks across the system. It's the bouncer logic behind 'Invalid API key'.
subsystems.psk_hierarchy: Maintains four shared-key families for household communication, control communication, room-name encryption and local-network swapping. Replicated settings identify the current and backup keys for each family. Rotation generates the replacements and commits the group together, with separate failures for key generation, encoding or updating settings and a network-settings version change. This keeps distinct uses from sharing one undifferentiated key. It does not establish that every player connection uses these keys or that every rotation is seamless for all peers.
subsystems.token_refresh: Coordinates music-account credential refresh with the transaction that needs the token. The operation can use a stored token, request a refresh, wait for a refresh already running and retry after successful completion. Account serial numbers associate the work with the right login. A missing service descriptor, missing transaction entry or a timed-out refresh produces a separate failure. The recovered states do not prove that one dedicated expiry-watching thread refreshes all credentials on a fixed schedule.
subsystems.registration: Maintains secure-registration state and its associated household and account-transfer information. It uses product-registration refresh and completion endpoints, accepts or clears an IPC-provided signing key and handles suspension, expiry, scheduled retry and errors. Conflicting household and local customer identifiers are detected rather than treated as equivalent identities. The record includes cloud exchanges as well as local state management, so it is not simply an on-network enrollment phase that always precedes a separate cloud registration.
subsystems.registration_machine: Runs the secure-registration attempts associated with registration-device certificate handling. It tracks state changes, suspension or expiry, success and error outcomes, and the next scheduled retry. A completion exchange uses a token, while signing-key data arrives through the local IPC path and is checked before being installed. New-certificate events supply the resulting device identity to other components, and transfer-state exit work has its own timed-job lifecycle. These are several coordinated transitions rather than one unconditional two-call success path.
subsystems.device_registration: Establishes or refreshes the player's secure registered-device identity through the household product endpoint. The recovered exchange has a refresh request and a completion request carrying a token, with state tracking for suspension, timeout, retries and errors. Certificate material can be flushed or invalidated, and household-customer conflicts and transfer-mode changes affect related handling. An unexpected authentication response is explicitly reported. These stages explain registration progress without treating an accepted request as an already-installed usable certificate.
subsystems.account_actions: The operations behind music-service account management: the routines that actually add, edit, and remove the saved logins for services like Spotify. They sit underneath the account commands documented on the service pages.
subsystems.account_migration: Converts saved music-service accounts to newer service identifiers or OAuth credential forms when the relevant migration path runs. The process can generate or refresh a token, request reauthentication or wait for a cloud connection, and it records attempts and failures. Related maintenance updates user information and per-account manifests. Entitlements also affect preinstalling Sonos Radio. Migration therefore has account-specific prerequisites and can require further work; it is not a guarantee that every login remains valid through every update.
subsystems.accounts_replication: Synchronizes saved music-service account records between household and cloud representations. Entries identify the service, account type, serial number and account identity and carry separate household and cloud revision clocks. Pull or push results can report an account added, updated, deleted, conflicted or rejected for missing or invalid metadata. Preferred-account selection is related but separate from merging records. The exact merge-predicate order remains unresolved, so the record does not guarantee that every newly added login is immediately usable in every room.
subsystems.alarm_clock: Manages alarm definitions and the timed work that requests their playback. Definitions include a start time, recurrence, duration and content, with validation for identifiers, recurrence, service content and the appropriate group role. Time-zone and internet-time handling supply the clock context, while clock-adjustment and synchronization failures are reported. Alarms can have silence, snooze or playback interactions beyond editing the stored list. A definition being saved and its playback being started are separate stages with separate errors.
subsystems.album_art: Resolves a requested artwork address and asks the image-streaming path to return the cover image. The worker records the source it is fetching and whether the image request failed. The associated /getaa proxy provides local controller-facing addresses, size variants and asynchronous request handling as documented in albumart_proxy. This lets metadata point at the speaker's image service without guaranteeing that every remote image is cached, available offline or faster to fetch through the proxy.
subsystems.areas: Stores named areas as sets of player identifiers in areas.json. Loading and saving use schema-version checks and staged file replacement, while mutations validate distinct identifiers, collection capacity and whether the area is read-only. A built-in Everywhere area has a fixed identity. These records describe an organizational set of players; creating an area is separate from starting playback or making those players one active playback group.
subsystems.autoplay: Automatically selects and starts an eligible source according to the player's configured room, grouping and volume choices. The recovered paths cover line-in-class sources including home-theater, AirPlay and Bluetooth variants carried through virtual-line-in state. Target resolution follows the room to its coordinator and control address, and invisible or incompatible players can be skipped. Missing source or control information can prevent the start. This is a source-and-target decision process rather than a universal instruction to play whenever any room becomes active.
subsystems.av_transport: Maintains the current playback source and coordinates play, pause, stop, skip, seek and source transitions through the applicable engine. Queue, cloud-queue, home-theater and virtual-line-in paths have their own work and state, alongside jobs for alarm duration, queue backup or radio metadata. A secondary group player cannot be treated as an independent coordinator for every source change. Errors, source capabilities and current group role determine what an operation can do, so one transport interface does not make every source behave identically.
subsystems.avt_impl: The implementation object behind the transport service: where the command routines' real work happens once the network layer has unpacked a request. The service page's commands all funnel into this object, which is the bridge between 'a network request arrived' and 'the transport engine did something'.
subsystems.avt_lastchange: Serializes transport state into the XML LastChange notification used by subscribed clients. The known values cover playing or paused state, play mode, track and source addresses, duration, metadata, available actions and transport-error details. Sonos extensions add direct-control identity, sleep-timer generation, restart, alarm and snooze status. A notification can contain multiple related values, while static NOT_IMPLEMENTED values indicate unavailable fields. Clients need to interpret the actual reported fields rather than assuming every update means a complete source change.
subsystems.browse_ids: Names the identifiers used to request music-service collections such as library artists, albums, tracks, playlists and stations. Other families select an artist's albums or top tracks, genre subcategories, recommendations or searches. These identifiers tell the service which collection to resolve; the returned entries still carry their own item identifiers and metadata. The vocabulary is service-specific and should not be treated as a guarantee that every provider implements every collection.
subsystems.browse_prefixes: Describes leading components of service content identifiers, such as playlist, artist-track, staff-pick, new-release and genre paths. The player uses those components to distinguish the kind of content or browsing request an identifier represents. They are parts of an object-address grammar, rather than evidence of an alphabetical jump index for names beginning with a chosen letter. The separate prefix-location commands have their own behavior and capability checks.
subsystems.catalog_translate: Asks a catalog-translation service to resolve an object identifier for a destination service. The request path includes the object identifier and destination-service identifier, and the wrapper rejects missing objectId, serviceId or targetObjectId information. A cached translation can be returned without another server connection; otherwise the response can be saved for later use. The cache lifetime remains unresolved. Finding a translation does not establish that all catalogs use one shared browse tree or that any two arbitrary items are equivalent.
subsystems.catalog_translation: Provides the cloud-backed identifier-mapping path also documented under catalog_translate. It validates the required object and service information, looks for a saved result and contacts the translation endpoint when no cached mapping is available. This can support resolving a reference in another service's identifier space. The returned mapping and that service's content availability still need to be checked; the feature does not automatically normalize every provider's catalog into an identical collection.
subsystems.content_directory: The music-library engine: it builds and holds the index of your shared music folders so 'browse by artist, album, genre' works without re-walking the shares every time. The library commands are its network face.
subsystems.customsd: Edits a custom music-service descriptor through the /customsd form. The descriptor supplies a service identifier, name, secure endpoint and polling interval, along with a sign-in method and capability choices such as search, playlists, logging or content filtering. Optional URLs provide strings, presentation instructions or a manifest. The form advertises custom identifiers 240 through 253 or 255, with 255 as its default, and a blank name erases the entry. This is music-service configuration rather than an alternative device-discovery protocol.
subsystems.didl_extractor: Reads playable-item metadata from DIDL-Lite XML and the player's additional metadata fields. Besides title, album and track number, the recovered vocabulary includes radio information, track gain, chapter position, advertisement markers, narrator and podcast identity, completion state and resume offsets. Resource protocol and content-type information help interpret the supplied playback address. Reading a field from metadata is separate from validating that its source can be played or that its value is present in every item.
subsystems.ext_audio_src: Runs queued auxiliary-audio jobs such as spoken responses, alerts, clips, setup chirps and discovery sounds. Jobs have identities and start, resume, cancellation or discard states, and exclusivity can defer or skip a competing job. The engine selects a compatible mixer stream, handles gain ramps and reports play-state changes. Unsupported sample rates, channel counts or decoder failures can prevent output. The job types do not establish that every sound overlays music or that ordinary physical line-in uses this same path.
subsystems.favorites: Maintains saved favorite references and their metadata, artwork addresses and update identifiers. Mutations persist the store and notify or replicate the changed information, while migration can rewrite older service references. Looking up a favorite can fail because its identifier, account information or item type cannot be resolved. These are stored references to content rather than copies of the underlying audio, so successfully saving an entry does not guarantee it remains playable later.
subsystems.group_mgmt: Applies a desired group membership by determining which players must join, leave or become standalone and which player should coordinate playback. The operation can copy an existing music context where the selected path permits it and can use a coordinator hint. Invalid member information, inconsistent topology, authorization or an uncopyable context can block the change; failed join or standalone operations can be retried. This is a multi-step transition, so the requested player list and the settled group state can differ while work is in progress.
subsystems.group_rc: Applies volume or mute changes to the local and remote members of a playback group. It tracks member volume, mute and fixed-output state and uses snapshots when calculating group adjustments. An operation can fail for all members, partially fail, overlap work already in progress or find that every member has fixed volume. Events track the requested group change and virtual-line-in completion. The remaining input to part of the volume calculation is unresolved, so this record does not specify one fully recovered numerical scaling formula.
subsystems.history_mgr: Buffers completed listening-history entries and communicates with the cloud history service. Entries need usable content and group information before submission; a full buffer or incomplete data can prevent them being queued. Reads use ETag and freshness information, with an explicit failure case when an unchanged server response leaves a corrupt local cache that cannot be served. Reading history is also gated by registration and history enablement. Cached availability, successful submission and complete history are therefore different outcomes.
subsystems.load_content: Resolves a selected container, stream, favorite, playlist or track list into the appropriate playback-loading path. The input carries a supported content type and metadata such as name, duration, artist or image information. Resolution can require a valid service/account association, and missing accounts, mismatched service identities or a full queue can stop loading. The verb family distinguishes loading tracks from loading a stream; selecting an item in a catalog is not proof that its resolved resource has begun playing.
subsystems.media_player_mgr: Tracks media-player actors using a target identity that includes the device, instance, port and secure-connection information. It can resolve an existing actor or backup, create and register an instance or report that none is available, with shutdown handled separately. Each instance also has its configuration and logging context. This identifies the object that should receive player work, while the per-operation socket encoding remains unresolved in the corresponding media-player protocol.
subsystems.mp_autoplay: Resolves where an incoming virtual-line-in source should start playing. It follows the configured target room to its coordinator and control address and applies choices for autoplay volume and included zones. Source types include home-theater, AirPlay and Bluetooth-related input classes, with a local fallback path for a lone line-in player. Invisible or incompatible players and missing target or coordinator information can prevent the operation. Several internal fields remain unnamed, so their values should not be assigned additional public meanings.
subsystems.mpmgr: Resolves a media-player instance from a target key containing device identity, instance, port and secure-connection choices. It detects overlapping registrations, can select an actor or backup and reports when no suitable actor exists. Instance creation, registration and shutdown have separate lifecycle steps, with virtual-line-in and volume callbacks attached to the selected player. This registry supports player-scoped work without proving that every modern-API operation must use it as its first validation step.
subsystems.music_accounts: Represents saved music-service logins using service and account identities, serial numbers, nicknames, tiers and credential metadata. Guest and linked-account paths have their own requirements, and malformed service identifiers or missing link, token or OAuth information can prevent an account operation. Checks also detect empty or duplicate account identities and can remove corrupt records. Replication and preferred-account selection are separate steps; finding an account in shared state does not alone prove its credentials are currently valid.
subsystems.music_services: Maintains the available music-service catalog in musicservices.xml and exposes versioned lists and descriptors to the rest of the player. Updates compare local and replicated versions, formats and last-updated information before accepting replacement data. Built-in services and downloaded descriptors can contribute entries, while a missing descriptor has its own warning. A catalog entry tells the player how a service is described; account authentication and successful content playback still have their own requirements.
subsystems.queue_schema: Describes queue diagnostics using separate capacity, current-use and high-water fields for entries and stored strings. The document also identifies the queue object, owner, update version, policy and any cloud-queue host. These fields let a reader distinguish a full queue from a queue whose contents simply changed. The actual maximums are supplied when the queue is created, and remaining string-table limits are still being traced rather than established as one universal constant.
subsystems.saved_queues: Stores saved Sonos queue references in savedqueues.rsq as a collection of queue identifiers and track URI/metadata records. The compressed representation carries version, next-identifier, curated status and declared track counts, which are checked when data is loaded or replicated. Writes use a temporary file and replacement or backup paths, and migration can update older service-account references. The saved file preserves a playlist description rather than copying its audio or guaranteeing that every referenced item remains available.
subsystems.share_indexer: Requests or performs indexing of configured network music shares so their tracks can be browsed by library attributes. Share records include a path, credentials, identifier and protocol-verification information; a resort request can become a full reindex where the selected path requires it. Diagnostics distinguish mounting or remote-share failures, local index-storage errors, cancellation and connection failures. The request to update the library, indexing progress and a successfully usable index are separate outcomes.
subsystems.sharelist: Maintains the configured network music-folder list and proposes versioned changes for replication between players. Add and remove operations validate paths, duplicate or overlapping shares, capacity and access, while protocol-verification results can cause unsupported entries to be removed. Local reindex and resort requests act on that configuration rather than creating a new share definition. Replication can reject a format mismatch or fail independently of saving a valid local list.
subsystems.svc_manifest: Downloads, stores, removes and replicates music-service manifest data, with saved metadata in svcmanifests.json. Parsing checks schema and API-version information and can reject an invalid identifier, URI or unsupported cloud-queue interface version. Stored versions and last-updated information let the player compare a manifest with a newer offered copy. This is additional service-description data, separate from the user's saved login and the actual media stream.
subsystems.topology_base: Tracks discovered players and updates their address, group, registration, idle and other reported attributes. Address-resolution checks can compare the expected IP and hardware identity, while unsuccessful discovery or trust checks can place a player in quarantine for later reconsideration. Events expose changes such as update availability or group membership. The remaining deactivation-state names and time-field encodings are still being traced, so those internal fields should not be assigned stronger public meanings.
subsystems.zone_topology: Maintains group relationships together with separate tracking for vanished and quarantined devices. A vanished record can retain its departure reason, battery information and time since disappearance; quarantine diagnostics instead describe discovery or admission failures and recheck state. Recovery work can attempt to wake missing bonded secondary speakers or process an unresponsive-device removal. These distinctions help explain an absent member without treating every missing player as the same network failure.
subsystems.zones_mgr: Applies zone-definition and membership changes, including joining, leaving, activating, deactivating or updating a zone. Primary and secondary players exchange channel-map information, and inconsistent definitions or unsupported home-theater primary changes can prevent the transition. Member-settings and zone-definition events notify other components of the changes. This connects the saved definition with the active relationship, rather than treating a file entry as an already-established bond.
subsystems.zones_storage: Persists zone definitions containing a name, identifier and channel map. Creation, update and removal have capacity and active-zone checks, while file loading validates the root object, data array and schema version. An offered replicated file must be renamed and loaded successfully; either step can fail or the schema can be rejected. Those outcomes distinguish data arriving from another player from the new definition being installed and used.
subsystems.zgs_mediaservers: Serializes the media-server section of ZoneGroupState. It lists server names, identities, locations and proxy URLs, together with service account counts and indexed account metadata such as nickname, serial number, tier and flags. The recovered field vocabulary also includes credential-related values, whose emission belongs to the particular serializer path. This section supplies structured server/account information; it should not be treated as proof that every credential field is present or every player is already authenticated to that service.
subsystems.zgt_schema: Defines the XML document used to report playback groups, their coordinators and member players. Player attributes can include identity, room name, software compatibility, channel maps, network state, orientation, calibration and registration information. Vanished and quarantined devices have separate sections with reason and last-known information. A reader must interpret which section and attributes are actually present; the schema vocabulary does not mean every model emits every hardware-related attribute.
subsystems.zgt_errors: The topology service's error layer: the error paths for unresponsive-device reports and malformed attribute requests. These are the error strings a bad topology request produces.
subsystems.rendering_control: Maintains per-zone and per-channel sound-control state, including volume, mute, gain, loudness and tuning choices. Deferred changes, overrides and ducking can alter the relationship between a requested volume and the level being applied to a source. The engine also handles ramps, scaling, persistent EQ and processing configuration and publishes related changes. A control-state update is therefore separate from the sample-processing or hardware step that produces the resulting sound.
subsystems.rc_impl: The rendering-control engine's event vocabulary: volume-changed, ducking, stereo-pair-state, and tuning-changed notifications the sound-control service publishes internally. It's the source of the updates apps see when the room's sound settings move.
subsystems.device_props: The device-properties internals: device-level attributes covering serial number, hardware address, display settings, button and light behavior, and infrared handling, plus the account-management commands. It's the 'who am I and how do I behave' layer of the speaker.
subsystems.smapi_client: The music-service client: the outbound side of service integration, covering session IDs, auth-token refresh, device auth tokens, and metadata fetching over each service's own interface. It's how the player logs into and talks to Spotify-style backends on your behalf.
subsystems.smapi_descriptor: Describes the configuration a music-service integration can declare, including its API key, presentation map, translated strings, browse and reporting information. Account-tier and capability fields indicate which sign-in or content interactions the service advertises, and flags can request device certificates, player context or authorization headers. These declarations let the player choose the appropriate integration path. A descriptor is separate from valid account credentials and is not, by itself, proof that every declared operation succeeds.
subsystems.wmp_provider: Browses and searches music shared by Windows Media Player. It asks for audio items, artists, albums, genres and playlists, then reads titles, playable resource URLs, durations, artist roles, album names and track numbers from the replies. Album listings request album and track-number ordering, and artwork uses either the server's album-art URL or the player's artwork proxy. This describes the provider's query and metadata conventions; an item returned by a search still needs a usable resource URL for playback.
subsystems.upnp_eventing: Maintains subscriptions through which other devices send changes to their control state. It records both a local subscription identifier and the identifier returned by the remote device, tracks the next renewal time and expected notification sequence, and counts renewal failures. Out-of-sequence notifications are recorded so a missing or unexpected update can be detected. Subscribe, renew and unsubscribe operations can fail, and the bookkeeping handles replies that arrive after a client has already been deleted. The subscription status page exposes these identifiers, renewal times and failure counts.
subsystems.upnputil: Shared control-protocol utilities: parsing host:port out of server addresses with strict validation, and mapping internal statuses to wire-level result codes. Small plumbing used across the classic command surface.
subsystems.acoustic_metrics: Defines the measurements attached to acoustic positioning results. They describe differences in sound arrival time, correlation peaks, confidence, signal and noise levels, and the shape and energy of a detected sound's leading edge. Other fields record measurement and retry counts, the orchestrator, debug data and result expiration. These values help assess whether a sound-based position estimate is credible; the field inventory alone does not establish how every measurement is calculated or which thresholds accept a result.
subsystems.addrmon: Listens for kernel messages about changes to IP addresses, bridge links and Wi-Fi activity. It translates an address addition or deletion into a player callback and forwards selected link and wireless messages to the same owner. That player callback can then update discovery advertisements or rebind connections. The monitor has one registered owner, rather than a separate subscriber list for each affected subsystem. Bridge-link messages are restricted to br0 and wireless messages to ath0; the IPv4 address parser resolves the interface name but does not apply the same name filter.
subsystems.arp_assoc: Tests whether local devices answer ARP requests and records repeated failures and subsequent recovery. Probes can run synchronously or asynchronously with configured intervals and timeouts; received data can request a timer reset, and an outstanding reset prevents another asynchronous start. The associated discovery tracker records timings and counts for controller discovery, ARP attempts and device-description requests, and suppresses invalid CrAssoc reports. These checks distinguish a local reachability failure from later discovery steps; they do not establish that a reachable device can play audio.
subsystems.boot_sequence: Reevaluates boot-related settings when events such as a Wi-Fi connection change occur. The settings include the target room name, local account-transfer mode, Wi-Fi and mesh disable flags, SonosNet disablement and the WEP key. Registered consumers apply the resulting configuration. The remaining investigation concerns which components participate in each pass; this record does not yet establish a complete startup order or prove that every pass ends with a household announcement.
subsystems.capability_guards: Rejects settings that require hardware features the target device lacks. Checks cover Ethernet with power-over-Ethernet support, a water sensor, a microphone switch, subwoofer status, suspension, a battery, Bluetooth, and a home-theater source with HDMI CEC. Battery-dependent settings also carry minimum and maximum battery percentages and a duration. A correctly formatted setting can therefore still be rejected on an unsuitable model. The concrete feature bitmasks for each product remain unresolved.
subsystems.cec_diagnostics: Lists the status and error fields used to describe a television's HDMI control and audio-return connection. They include TV and device CEC status, TV power status, System Audio Mode state and error, ARC state and error, TV error, eARC activity, and audio/video test fields. These fields let diagnostics distinguish control-channel, audio-return and TV-side conditions. Their names identify the reported categories, but this record does not yet decode all numeric states or explain every error trigger.
subsystems.common_logger: Configures how diagnostic messages are filtered, formatted and stored. Settings select category filters, a default level, file and preserved sizes, backups, standard-error output and an optional network host and port. Log lines include a source label, timestamp and severity information. Invalid category names and file read or status failures are reported, and the recovered message vocabulary includes network, settings and JSON parsing errors. The record documents the shared configuration and output conventions; it does not prove that every subsystem uses every destination.
subsystems.cpu_monitor: Reads per-core CPU counters from /proc/stat and reports user, system, idle and software-interrupt activity, alongside interrupt and timing information. It detects cores that have entered a shutdown state and guards percentage calculations against zero denominators and overflow. These readings help explain whether a player is busy or idle. The recovered code does not establish that this monitor itself throttles background jobs or changes audio scheduling.
subsystems.crash_report: Reports crash events with the process name, crash count, whether the player crashed, lifetime and the upload response. It records whether reporting succeeded or failed. This is the event-reporting record associated with a crash; the fields shown here do not establish which logs or stack dumps are attached, nor that a failed submission will automatically be retried.
subsystems.csfcm: This keeps a short history of audio-stream bookmarks so the player can recover the correct stream position for a playback time. It stores at most128 distinct contexts, avoids adding consecutive identical bookmarks, and preserves a marked boundary during cleanup. If the history fills up, it stops accepting and returning contexts until flushing clears the exhaustion state; playback recovery can then fall back to the latest saved position.
subsystems.daemon_ipc: The request-forwarding table that lets this program ask its sibling system daemons to do things: the power coordinator, the Bluetooth manager, the LED manager, and the network-startup process, plus the answers those requests can return. It's the inter-process glue of the appliance.
subsystems.dataio: Provides HTTP transport for downloading or exchanging data. It reads response status, content type, cookies, cache lifetimes, modification dates, entity tags and authentication challenges, and supports SSL reads and writes. Its response parser checks header boundaries and decodes chunked bodies, rejecting oversized lengths, invalid hexadecimal chunk sizes and broken terminators. Callers can wait for available bytes, but a closed socket, timeout, malformed response or request beyond the available data can fail the operation. This is network transport, rather than a general serializer for records stored on disk.
subsystems.datatap: Captures a snapshot of data retained by an internal tap. The generic tap handles capture metadata and snapshot output; the rolling-audio subtype retains recent audio in a circular buffer. For the SPDIF capture path, the player stages a file, exports its contents as base64 inside an SPDIFTap XML element and removes the staged file afterward. Snapshot creation can fail after writing only part of the data. Some capture-format fields remain unidentified, so the snapshot should not be treated as an ordinary playable audio file.
subsystems.desired_settings: Stores requested clock and scheduling values separately from the values currently in effect. Requests include time and date display formats, the time server, the desired time and its time zone, household UTC time, and the daily music-index refresh time. The settings manager applies these requests and updates the corresponding current values. A requested value therefore describes intended configuration rather than proof that the clock or schedule has already changed; the recovered fields do not establish a general rollback guarantee.
subsystems.dev_disc: Receives local-network discovery searches and alive or departure announcements, including Sonos controller announcements. It records source addresses and lost SSDP messages, handles quarantine rechecks, and builds signed responses to discovery searches. Sonos-specific headers carry household identity, secure device-description locations and controller session information. Discovery can fail through socket setup, response-signing or manifest-loading errors, and service-manifest URLs must use HTTPS. An announcement identifies a discovery event; it does not by itself prove that the device is authenticated or ready for playback.
subsystems.devmode: Enables selected development capabilities using a signed statement file. Each statement identifies a capability and an applicable software-version range; updates are staged before loading, then listeners and other processes are notified of changes. Some statements may persist across boots, while permission to install an SSH public key is explicitly barred from persistence. Signature verification and per-statement policy therefore govern access. The recovered mechanism does not establish that development mode is always off on every production player.
subsystems.diagnostics: Coordinates a diagnostic submission across players and, when requested, controllers. It creates a versioned manifest, starts a submission with the player serial number, distributes a diagnostic identifier, asks devices to collect their reports and waits for submission results. Reports include software, network and quarantine information; unavailable devices can be represented by stub support documents with hashes. Progress records distinguish all devices reporting from a timeout, and confirmation identifiers are checked against the expected submission. A diagnostic request can therefore complete with missing or stubbed devices rather than a complete report from every player.
subsystems.download_status: Names the outcomes of a file download: not yet called, in progress, succeeded, or unchanged, plus write, truncation, size, file and connection errors. This vocabulary lets a caller distinguish an active transfer from a finished one and identify whether failure came from the connection or the file being produced. An unchanged result is separate from downloading a new file; the enumeration does not by itself define retry behavior.
subsystems.drm_content_keys: Reads content-key descriptors supplied in music-service track metadata, including Apple Music StoreKit-style key references. A keyed table detects duplicate entries, and the playback request carries an X-Sonos-Playback-Id header to identify the playback session. Device-token requests also check the account credential type. These metadata entries describe how protected content obtains its keys; they are not themselves a persistent store of decrypted keys.
