index.intro: This reference explains the control interfaces and internal components recovered from specific Sonos firmware builds. The primary target is the model-9 player running build 86.10-80260. Plain-English descriptions explain behavior and practical quirks; technical sections retain addresses, field layouts, call chains and supporting artifacts. Evidence ranges from complete function traces to inventories of strings or tables, so each record must be read at its stated scope. Remaining unknowns are recorded as TODOs rather than assumed away.
index.counts: The counts below distinguish three things that are easy to conflate, and conflating them is exactly how 'the speaker has 205 commands' myths start. First: what the product's specification documents promise. Sonos ships each player with small description files listing the commands it claims to support. That's the advertised surface, and it can over-promise, because a command can stay in the spec after the code behind it was removed. Second: what the player actually dispatches, meaning the commands a request will really reach code for. Third: what that code does. A few advertised commands are wired to empty routines that accept your request and change nothing, and a few more reject every call with an error. This site tracks all three layers separately, so for every command you can see whether it's genuinely live, a stub that does nothing, or a ghost that only exists in the paperwork.

architecture.intro: How a network command reaches real code. When a control message arrives at the player it doesn't land on one dedicated function. Instead it passes through a layered routing system where it is parsed, looked up by name, validated, and finally handed to the code that does the work. This page maps that journey and the machinery on each step.
architecture.routing: The tables below are the player's URL map for control traffic. Each row is one service address, meaning the path part of the URL the command is sent to, like a postal code for which department should open the letter. When a request arrives, the player matches its destination against this map to find the right service object, and from there the per-service command table takes over. Seeing all the addresses in one place is the clearest proof of which services genuinely exist on this firmware: anything missing here can't be reached no matter what the spec documents say.
architecture.request_vtable: Every inbound SOAP command is wrapped in the same temporary TRequest object before the service code sees it. Think of it as shared request plumbing: it walks the command's input fields in their declared order, creates slots for output values, runs the common validation path, sends SOAP faults, and serializes the final response. The action handler still decides what the command actually does; TRequest makes the input/output and error handling consistent across services.
architecture.capability_fields: The player keeps internal switches that decide which features exist on this particular hardware or in this mode: a capabilities checklist consulted at runtime. Some commands read these switches before doing anything. A feature may be compiled into the firmware but disabled on this model, or enabled only while a certain mode is active. This is why 'the command exists' doesn't always mean 'the command works', because a switch can make an otherwise-live command refuse to run.
architecture.internal_functions: Named helper routines the command routines share, which form the common toolbox: argument parsers that turn text fields into numbers, validators that enforce ranges and required values, and error translators that turn internal result codes into proper network error replies. Listing them matters because they're the vocabulary every routine speaks. Once you know these helpers, you can predict how any command will react to malformed input.
architecture.dispatch_candidates: Functions we investigated because they looked like command routers: the routines that might have been the switchboard steering incoming commands to the code that runs them. Most turned out to be something else. The survivors are documented here with the evidence for and against.
architecture.shared_subsystems: Shared components interpret content references, parse metadata, schedule work, move audio between players, manage stored configuration and assemble reports. Their records explain the inputs, state changes, outputs and failure conditions established by the recovered evidence. Related service records identify where commands use them, without implying that understanding one shared helper resolves every caller.

availability.intro: The complete command surface in one table: every action the firmware can route to real code, alongside whether it actually works. For each command you can see whether it's advertised to apps, whether calling it does anything, and how confident we are in that verdict.

state_variables.intro: State variables describe values exposed by the player, including playback state, source references, volume settings, group identity and collection revisions. The records identify types, output forms and recovered producers where available. Some values are constants or snapshots; others appear inside bundled change documents. A reported setting is distinct from a successful operation or audible result, and not every variable has its own independent notification.

events.intro: The player can send state through classic UPnP subscriptions and named WebSocket event channels. Classic notifications wrap properties in XML, and selected services bundle state into LastChange documents. WebSocket subscriptions expose named feeds. Delivery depends on registration, permission, connection state and renewal; these mechanisms do not guarantee one immediate message for every underlying change.
events.wss_registry: Lists the named feeds recovered for WebSocket subscriptions, including playback, grouping and settings-related state. A channel name identifies a subscription topic, not a complete payload schema or proof that every client uses it. Its implementation and connection policy determine when updates are available.
events.gena_internals: How the classic notification mechanism is implemented on this player: what happens when an app subscribes (how the player validates the request, assigns the subscription, and remembers where to send updates), how a state change becomes a notification message, and how renewals and timeouts keep the subscription list clean. This is the machinery behind 'your app updates the moment the volume changes'.
events.per_service: Shows recovered notification behavior by service, including which services emit a LastChange document. That document bundles state values and can include unchanged or fixed fields, rather than serving as a chronological log of only the latest edits. Other services use ordinary property notifications.

services.AVTransport: The busiest event source in the system. Every play, pause, skip, seek, queue change, and mode change announces itself here, bundled into a LastChange document so a track change plus a state change arrive as one update instead of two. This is the feed that keeps the app's now-playing screen live.
services.AlarmClock: Fires when the alarm list or household time settings change: a new alarm, an edit, a deletion, a timezone change. Apps holding the alarm screen open refresh off this feed.
services.AudioIn: Registered but silent on this build. The whole AudioIn service is a reject-everything stub, so nothing here ever emits an event, matching the dead commands.
services.ConnectionManager_server: The library-side connection service's notifications, fired when connections open or close against the music-library side of the player. Routine plumbing that apps rarely subscribe to. Since this player has no content to prepare for others, the updates here are mostly bookkeeping rather than the busy list seen on the renderer side.
services.ContentDirectory: Fires when the music library changes: a rescan finishing, an object created or destroyed, the library version ticking up. It's the 'your music changed, refresh the browse view' signal.
services.DeviceProperties: Fires when device settings change: LED on/off, button lock, room name or attributes, bonded-zone changes. It's the feed behind a settings screen updating itself when something else edits the speaker.
services.GroupManagement: Fires when group membership changes: a speaker joining or leaving the group, or source-area updates. It's the feed that keeps a multi-room view correct while people regroup rooms.
services.GroupRenderingControl: Fires when the group-level volume or mute changes. This is the event feed behind the group volume slider and group mute button updating in real time everywhere.
services.HTControl: Fires when home-theater control state changes: IR repeater toggled, remote learned, LED feedback switched. It lets an app watch the home-theater settings (remote-learning state, TV autoplay, LED feedback) as they change, though it fires rarely and is mostly for the settings screens.
services.MusicServices: Fires when the music-service list or account sessions change: a service added or removed, a session refreshed. Primarily it carries the available-services version, so apps refresh when the catalog of services changes.
services.QPlay: The QPlay service's event surface, part of the Tencent QQ Music integration. It's silent on builds where that feature isn't active, which is nearly everywhere.
services.Queue: Fires when a managed queue changes: tracks added, removed, reordered, or a queue created or destroyed. It's the internal feed the system's own components follow when watching queue edits.
services.RenderingControl: The volume and tone feed. Every volume move, mute, and bass/treble/loudness change announces here, bundled into LastChange so the app's slider tracks whatever anyone else does, including the physical buttons on the unit.
services.SystemProperties: Fires when a settings-store key or an account credential changes, which is the 'some configuration was edited' signal other features watch. It carries the stored-settings version stamps for configuration like voice IDs or the service map.
services.VirtualLineIn: Fires when a virtual line-in session changes: a feed starting or stopping, or its transport state moving. It's relevant only while an external source is pushing audio.
services.ZoneGroupTopology: The household-shape feed: it fires whenever the map of the system changes, covering a speaker appearing or disappearing, rooms grouping or ungrouping, and coordinators changing. It's the most important subscription for anything rendering the whole-system view.
services.ConnectionManager_renderer: The playback-side connection service's notifications, fired when control connections open or close against the player. Routine plumbing like its library-side sibling, and the feed behind 'who is talking to this player right now'.

errors.intro: What a failed command actually returns. When a request goes wrong, whether a missing argument, a value out of range, or a command that doesn't exist, the player answers with a standardized fault message carrying a numeric error code. Some codes mean the same thing everywhere in the system (bad arguments are always the same number), while others are service-specific or internal error codes leaking out. This page documents the fault format itself, every code the firmware is proven to emit, and for each command the specific set of errors it can produce. That last part is often the most useful, since 'what can go wrong' is as much of an interface as 'what it does right'.
errors.wire_format: The exact structure of a failure reply, meaning the envelope a fault travels in. One detail worth knowing: only the error number is machine-checked by the player. The human-readable message beside it is decorative, and some errors carry deliberately unhelpful text. So when you see a fault, trust the number, not the words.
errors.vocabulary: Every numeric error code proven to be emittable by this firmware. The standard ranges cover common meanings like invalid action, missing argument, and value out of range, while higher numbers encode Sonos-specific failures: wrong playback mode for this source, optimistic-concurrency clashes on queue edits, and feature-not-implemented on this model. Where a code's meaning was recovered from the binary rather than the public spec, that's noted.
errors.per_action: For each command, the union of error codes it can actually produce: everything its routine, argument validation, and internal machinery can emit, not just the generic set. This is the practical section, because 'what can this specific command fail with' is what a real client needs to handle.

uri_formats.intro: Documents resource references recognized or produced by the player, including queues, saved playlists, inter-room streams, music-service objects and calibration assets. Each format identifies its components and recovered parser or emitter behavior. Some entries are type labels, unused literals or references requiring further resolution, rather than direct audio URLs. Known grammar and unresolved field meanings are stated separately.

payload_formats.intro: Explains structured values carried in strings, files or messages: metadata XML, persisted records, bookmarks, timestamps and capability flags. The records distinguish what a producer writes from what a parser accepts and note quirks such as ignored trailing text or partially updated state after failure. A recovered format is not automatically a complete account of its consumers or runtime policy.

http_api.intro: Beyond the documented control surface, the player answers ordinary HTTP requests: a built-in diagnostic and maintenance web surface most users never see. Some of it is famous. The /status page gives a rich snapshot of what the player is doing, and the support tools lean on it heavily. But there are also endpoints for rebooting, managing logs, checking network state, and a few surprising extras. This page inventories every HTTP path the firmware registers: what's served, what it accepts, and which of them are genuinely useful versus internal.

firmware.intro: Compares selected firmware builds and models using recovered strings, tables, code and shipped files. Presence of a literal is different from a reachable implementation, and the strength of each comparison depends on its evidence. Product and version differences limit which findings transfer to another player; a shared version number does not imply identical hardware or behavior.
firmware.product_surface: Across the builds compared, every player advertises the same set of service documents with the same command lists, so the advertised surface is remarkably stable. The interesting differences hide underneath: which commands are actually implemented, which routines do real work, and which features exist on which models. The spec is a veneer; this section is about what's behind it on each build.
firmware.service_matrix: A literal check of which service identifiers exist in each build: a simple present/absent matrix showing what the firmware added or dropped across versions and models. It's the quickest way to see, for example, which builds carry the QPlay integration or the virtual line-in service.
firmware.entries: Records individual differences with the compared builds and the evidence for each. A changed string can establish a vocabulary difference, while a function trace or artifact comparison can support a stronger behavioral conclusion. The explanation keeps those levels separate instead of treating every added name as a completed new feature.

entry_text.QPlay service URN literal: The QPlay service, the Tencent QQ Music casting integration, exists only in certain builds. Its identifier string is present in this firmware, proving the feature shipped here even though most markets never saw it. Other builds lack the string entirely, showing where the integration was added or dropped.
entry_text.VirtualLineIn service: The virtual line-in service, meaning the control surface for externally-pushed audio, appears in some builds and not others. Its presence tracks which firmware can host push-style sessions like a music service's own direct-streaming.
entry_text.sonos-com ContentDirectory namespace: The music-library service carries a Sonos-specific extension namespace on some builds, meaning extra commands beyond the standard set. Which builds carry it marks where Sonos extended the standard library protocol with their own commands.
entry_text./status/opt/log/mdnsd.log: One diagnostic HTTP path found in some builds: an endpoint that serves the multicast-discovery daemon's log. It's useful for debugging 'speakers can't see each other' problems, and it's present only on certain firmware.
entry_text./device_account registration subroutes: Some builds expose extra web endpoints under device-account registration, which is part of the account-linking flow where a speaker registers itself against Sonos's cloud. Which routes exist changed across versions as that flow evolved.
entry_text./api route: The presence of the top-level /api mount (the front door of the modern REST API) differs across builds. It marks exactly which firmware generation introduced the modern app-facing interface alongside the classic command surface.
entry_text.FV token grammar: The format of an authentication token used in API access changed across builds, meaning the grammar of the credential string the modern API checks. It's a small but real security-relevant difference between versions.
entry_text.x-sonos-* header set: The family of custom HTTP headers the firmware recognizes grew across builds. These headers carry Sonos-specific request metadata, and each addition is evidence of a new cross-device feature riding on the HTTP layer.
entry_text.x-sonosapi-iqradio scheme: The iqradio and iqradioinst address labels occur in the compared 34.16 binary and are absent from the later binaries examined. This establishes a change in the stored service-address vocabulary. It does not identify every provider or prove that the absence of those names removed all related playback behavior.
entry_text.x-rincon-stream / x-sonosapi-show / true: The compared builds use different inter-room and calibration reference forms. The later binaries contain a parameterized stream selector, show references and OGG calibration-tone names, while older ones contain a WAV stream form and different tone filenames. These differences identify format and asset conventions, rather than proving an entire feature was newly introduced.
entry_text.x-rincon-enc2: The enc2 label was found in the compared model-9 86.8 binary. Its presence distinguishes that image's protected-content vocabulary. The literal alone does not establish a second-generation stream protocol, its encoding fields or an active consumer.
entry_text.explicitContentFiltering config key: The explicit-content-filtering setting name appears in the compared 57.10 and later binaries. It identifies configuration used by content-filtering behavior. Presence of the key is separate from the setting being enabled or every source enforcing the same restriction.
entry_text.int_setTransferMode: The internal transfer-mode key was found only in the compared 86.10-80260 binary. This records a vocabulary difference between the sampled builds. Without its producer and consumer behavior, the name does not establish a network-protocol rewrite or explain the mode's complete purpose.
entry_text.RINCON metadata NS additions: The later metadata vocabulary adds advertisement, link URL and track-gain fields, while the older preset field disappears from the sampled string set. Other metadata names remain stable. These comparisons show available field names, rather than proving every item supplies them or every client understands them.
entry_text./status route table: The diagnostic web surface's route table (the list of /status pages the player serves) differs between builds, showing which diagnostics each generation exposed.
entry_text.SystemProperties removed actions: Two SystemProperties commands (ProvisionCredentialedTrialAccountX and ResetThirdPartyCredentials) are still advertised in this build's spec but have no implementation. They're the 'ghost' entries, and comparing builds shows when each died.
entry_text.Muse software-update REST surface restru: The modern API's software-update routes were restructured between builds: the endpoints apps use to check for and trigger updates were reorganized, marking a change in how firmware updates are driven.
The shared plumbing of the modern API moved build trees between versions. It's an internal restructuring visible in the binaries' own record of where code came from.
entry_text.RMuseFeature flag additions: Later builds contain additional feature names for hardware status, generated sound, temperature or home-theater telemetry, LAN swapping and selected settings. These names identify new configuration or capability vocabulary. Each flag's actual effect and whether it is enabled require its consumer evidence.
entry_text.Group-forming ungroupable-player guards: Later builds add guards preventing certain players from forming groups. It's a restriction for models that can't lead or join in some modes, and it's absent from older firmware.
entry_text.Bundled curl upgrade (DoH + HTTPS-RR + h: The newer binary contains additional HTTP-client vocabulary for DNS-over-HTTPS, HTTPS resource records, competing connection attempts, alternate services and HTTP/3-related handling. This establishes that newer library mechanisms are present. It does not prove that every mechanism is enabled or that each outgoing request uses it successfully.
entry_text.Playback-state guard additions: Extra checks added around playback state in newer builds: stricter validation before transport commands are allowed to proceed, marking tightened state machinery over time.
entry_text.rootfs content diff: fenway (m8) vs lime: The version-matched Play:1 and Playbar filesystems differ in decoder libraries, infrared support, DSP data, calibration assets and recovery scripts. Their flash layouts differ too, and the same reset-check result selects different reset severity in the two boot scripts. A shared software version therefore does not establish identical components or reset behavior across models.
entry_text.anacapad binary .rodata diff: m8/fenway: The compared Playbar binary contains richer TV-input, decoder, master transmission and woofer-array vocabulary, while the Play:1 binary contains satellite receiving and other product DSP personalities. The differences show distinct source and sink roles within the shared firmware family. String comparisons establish those code and data families without proving every named path is active.

subsystems.intro: Describes the player's audio, networking, discovery, storage, calibration, reporting and maintenance components. Each explanation identifies what the component handles, what it changes or produces, and the conditions or failures that matter. Detailed evidence remains with the technical record. Some entries are inventories or partial traces, so the page does not claim that every subsystem has been completely reversed.

muse.intro: Documents the recovered Muse resource vocabulary and operations alongside the detailed technical evidence for routes and message handling. Public descriptions explain what each resource requests or reports without assuming how every app uses it. A route or operation name is distinct from a working feature on this model, and requests must be distinguished from completed state changes.
muse.description: Every route is registered as a small record holding three things: the URL pattern (with placeholders like a player ID), which HTTP methods it accepts, and a machine-name string naming the operation. Most operations exist in two spellings, one addressing a single player directly and one going through the household, which is why the route count is nearly double the operation count. The tables below are the complete recovered route registry.
muse.flags_decode: Each route carries a bitmask saying which HTTP verbs it accepts (GET for reads, POST for creates, PUT and PATCH for edits, DELETE for removals) plus a marker dividing 'settings' operations from 'playback' operations. That division turns out to be meaningful, because the pipeline treats the two classes differently when checking permissions.
muse.dispatch: Every route funnels into one shared router: a single front door that all API traffic passes through. Two thin entry points merely record which channel the request arrived on (local network versus the cloud tunnel) before joining the same machinery, so every operation sees a uniform request no matter where it came from.
muse.tables: Routes are registered in two dialect tables: one phrased in terms of household IDs (the cloud-flavored form, where requests name the household and the player inside it) and one in player IDs (the local form used on your home network). The same operation appears in both, which is why the tables look like near-copies of each other.
muse.op_spine: Every operation is a small object built from the same template: a shared 'may I run?' check, its own execute step that does the real work, and a ladder of optional hooks. The early hooks read fields out of the request body (each overridden hook corresponds to one declared parameter), and the later hooks build whatever internal request the operation forwards to the player's engines. Reading which hooks each operation overrides is exactly how each command's parameter list was recovered.
muse.validation_lib: Before any operation runs, a shared validation library checks the request body field by field for missing required fields, wrong types, out-of-range values, and unknown fields that shouldn't be there. It's the same idea as the argument checking on the classic command surface, just generalized for JSON documents: every operation gets uniform, thorough input checking without implementing it itself.
muse.pipeline: The gauntlet each API request runs before it reaches real work: the incoming HTTP request is unpacked, its content type checked, the caller's credentials verified, the URL's numeric placeholders parsed, the body decoded as JSON and validated field-by-field, and only then does the operation's own execute step run. Each stage can reject the request with its own error before any music-relevant code is touched, which is why the API fails so uniformly: the failures all happen here, not in the operations.
muse.request_envelope: Stage one: the incoming HTTP request is unpacked into a working context made of headers, flags, and a scratch space the later stages fill in. From here on, the request is a structured object, not raw text.
muse.content_type: Stage two: requests carrying a body must declare they're sending JSON, and edit operations (PATCH) additionally demand the merge-patch content type. Wrong or missing declarations are rejected here, because the API refuses to guess what format a body is in.
muse.auth: Stage three: an API-key check guards the whole surface. A missing or wrong key fails with 'Invalid API key' before anything else is examined, making it the bouncer at the door of the modern API. On local requests the check is typically satisfied by the household's own credentials, and it's what stops arbitrary network neighbors from driving your speakers.
muse.path_params: Stage four: numeric placeholders in the URL (the player, group, and household IDs embedded in the path) are parsed as integers. A non-numeric or malformed ID is rejected here, before it can confuse an operation.
muse.body: Stage five: the JSON body is decoded into a working store, the structured document the operation's parameter hooks will read from. Malformed JSON fails here, and then the field-by-field validation library checks what was decoded.
muse.errors: How pipeline failures are reported: each stage can abort with its own status code and error string before the operation ever runs. That's why API errors are so uniform: they all come from this shared gauntlet, not from the operations themselves.
muse.op_dispatch: Stage six: with everything validated, the named operation's own execute method finally runs. This is the stage that actually does the work, reading its parameters from the body store via its hooks and forwarding the real request to the player's engines.
muse.outbound: The player is also a client of this same API: it builds these very calls itself toward other players and toward the cloud, for features like group volume fan-out and household coordination. The outbound vocabulary and request-building machinery lives here, showing the same API from the sender's side.
muse.field_vocab: The request and response field names each API namespace works with: the vocabulary of the JSON documents flowing through the routes, covering which keys appear in playback commands, group settings, and alarm edits. Field names matter because they're the real API contract, meaning the strings an app actually sends.
muse.event_channels: Lists named event topics associated with the Muse interface. They allow a subscriber to receive selected state updates over the relevant connection. A topic name alone does not establish the full message shape, permission requirements or delivery timing.
muse.resources: Lists the 67 resource groups represented in this dataset, such as playback, alarms, devices, volume and calibration. Their descriptions name the recovered operations and scope. This is a map of the recovered interface, rather than proof that every operation is available to every client or implemented on every product.
muse.unresolved: What remains open on this page. The structure is fully recovered (every route, every operation, every hook), but the honest gap is human-readable intent for a few operations: we know the mechanics (what fields it reads, what it forwards) without a name that says what it's for in plain terms. Where that's the case, the entry says so rather than inventing a label.

family_text.playback: Playback controls, source loading, session membership, metadata and sleep timers. These resources distinguish requesting playback, describing it and observing its state; source resolution and session progress can still fail.
family_text.volume-home-theater: Player and group volume, temporary ducking, home-theater options, accessory state and HDMI diagnostics. Hardware support and current topology determine which operations apply. Pinewood names remote-like controls rather than a proven satellite handshake.
family_text.audio-input: The line-in and AirPlay-style input surface: virtual line-in sources exposed as streams other players can subscribe to. The JSON counterpart of the VirtualLineIn service.
family_text.households-zones: Household identity, area and zone definitions, active zones and playback-group membership. Stored organization and a live group are different layers; changing a definition does not prove a completed join or synchronized playback.
family_text.alarms-timers: Alarm objects, snoozing, timer lifecycle and sleep-timer configuration. Scheduling or saving a request is separate from reaching its deadline and successfully performing the later action.
family_text.content: Library shares and indexing, service-content translation, saved references, playlists, history and entitlements. These resources manage descriptions and access context; they do not store copies of every referenced audio resource.
family_text.calibration: Speaker presence, acoustic signalling, positioning measurements, calibration configuration and status. The recovered operations expose parts of the measure-and-tune flow without proving that every calibration method runs on this model.
family_text.settings: Player settings and their effective resolved values: names, EQ, LED state, button lock, loudness and the rest. The effectiveSettings resource is a read-mostly merged view the firmware computes over several backing stores. SystemProperties covers a slice of this over SOAP.
family_text.device-hardware: Device registration and status, hardware readings, power policy and infrared configuration. The shared vocabulary spans products with different sensors and connectors, so an operation name is separate from local hardware support.
family_text.voice-control: Voice-account linking and onboarding plus a virtual-button command. Account state, physical microphone support and the result of a control request are distinct facts.
family_text.system: Player and household update requests and status, diagnostics, selected system reports, network tests and time-related operations. These are several maintenance interfaces, rather than one guaranteed path for every internal task.
family_text.authorization: The auth surface: token issuance and revocation, household membership proofs and the lechmere policy checks every other resource is gated behind. This is the mechanism that decides which app on which account may call which op.
family_text.upnp-bridge: A mechanical bridge layer: each resource here forwards muse calls into the matching local UPnP service, so an app can drive the classic SOAP action set through the JSON API without speaking SOAP. The op names map almost one-to-one onto SCPD actions, which is why these pages look repetitive; the interesting part is that the bridge exists at all.

artifacts.intro: Lists the firmware artifacts included in this research, such as executable files, configuration, audio assets and web documents. Entries record origin, size, checksum and recovered role where available. These files provide inspectable evidence for the analysis, but the inventory should not be treated as a claim that every file from every firmware image is published here.

muse_spec_streams.intro: Behind the modern REST API there is a catalog that spells out, for every operation, exactly which fields a request or response may carry and what type each field is. This page is that catalog, listed raw. Each section is one cluster of related operations (the verb names printed beside it), and each row inside is a field name paired with the type the firmware expects for it. Rows marked 'globalError' name the error shapes an operation can hand back, and rows marked 'upnpEvent' describe payloads the speaker pushes out to subscribers on its own rather than returning when asked. It is dense reading, but it is the ground truth for anyone building or studying a client for the API.

soap.intro: This is the classic UPnP control surface: the seventeen SOAP services the speaker advertises (plus the hidden ones it doesn't), every action they accept, every state variable they publish, and the wire rules that govern all of it. Each service gets its own page with a friendly walkthrough of what the actions actually do, followed by the reverse-engineered evidence: handler addresses, dispatch records, argument types, validation, and fault codes. The supporting pages cover the shared machinery underneath: how GENA eventing and LastChange documents push state to subscribers, the full fault-code vocabulary, the URI schemes used in SetAVTransportURI and friends, the opaque payload dialects embedded inside XML fields, and an action-by-action availability matrix across the whole surface.

open_work.intro: Collects subsystem records with remaining TODOs and links to their full evidence. Each nonempty TODO identifies unresolved work; a complete record has no TODO field. This page covers the records selected by its generator, rather than every possible unknown in the firmware.
